steps.content: The idea is about a single day's close relative to its open: when a coin closes well above where it started, it should keep rising. So the raw quantity is the daily log return, and the direction is positive. I'll start with the simplest form: the 5-day average of that log return.<function_calls>test_factor(expression="Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('open')) - 1").ln().ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)")</function_calls>

The idea says a big drop yesterday predicts a bounce, so the factor should rise when yesterday's return was large in magnitude but negative. I'll start with the simplest form: minus the negative part of yesterday's return, which is the largest drop and is the direction the idea asks for.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 907 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0025
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0051 (t = -3.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0049, 2023 -0.0060, 2024 -0.0042

The simplest version comes out negative and consistent across all three periods (t = −3.1), so the bounce idea doesn't hold as stated — the raw magnitude of yesterday's drop carries reversal, not a bounce. Before concluding, I'll test whether the effect is specific to the size of the move (big drops bouncing harder) by dividing yesterday's return by its own absolute value, which is bounded and less dominated by volatility.
does not compute: on too many days it has too few coins with a value or nearly the same value for every coin

The bounded ratio collapses to a constant for every coin, so it is not informative — I'll drop that. Instead I'll ask whether the effect is a *recent* habit rather than one day's reversal, by taking the largest drop over the last five days.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0094
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0089 (t = -4.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0145, 2023 -0.0081, 2024 -0.0068

Five-day average of the same quantity is even more negative (−0.0089, t = −4.3), so the habit form is worse than the one-day version. That is two tests in a row that failed to improve on the first result, so I'll stop and hand in the simplest tested form.

What I found: the idea does not hold on this history. A coin whose return yesterday was the worst of its recent ones — i.e. a coin that fell a lot yesterday — tends to do *worse* over the next days, not better, and the sign is stable in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 (t ≈ −3.1). Dividing yesterday's return by its own absolute value was a dead end because that ratio is constant for every coin, and averaging the same quantity over five days made it more negative (−0.0089), so the effect is one-day reversal rather than a bounce. I kept the direction the idea asks for, so the factor is the largest negative drop, which is negative-IC by construction.

The idea is about the daily high-low range being bearish, so the factor should be negative of the range. The range is `high - low` in price units, which is already unit-free and comparable across coins. I'll start with the simplest form: the log of the range, averaged over a short window.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0614
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0203 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190

The simple version works well: incremental IC +0.0203 with t = 8.7 and the same sign in all three periods. Now I'll check whether the effect is better captured as a persistent property of the coin — the typical range over a longer window — rather than a recent one, since the idea says "wide range tends to fall afterwards" and "tends" suggests persistence.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0521
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0108 (t = 4.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0122, 2023 +0.0066, 2024 +0.0142

The longer-window median is weaker (+0.0108 vs +0.0203), so the recent range is the right part of the signal. One more form to check: ranking each day's range across coins first and then averaging, which ignores the magnitude of the range and asks "is this coin wide relative to other coins today" — that is a different shape of the same idea.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0591
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0190 (t = 7.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0295, 2023 +0.0143, 2024 +0.0185

The cross-sectional rank form lands at +0.0190, below the +0.0203 of the plain log-range mean, so two forms in a row have failed to improve — time to stop and hand in the best one.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Coins whose recent daily high-low range is wide go on to underperform, and the sign is the same in all three sub-periods, which the other forms lacked. The effect is strongest when the range is measured as the log of high/low and averaged over the last five days: incremental IC +0.0203 with t = 8.7, positive in 2022H2 (+0.0305), 2023 (+0.0164) and 2024 (+0.0190). Averaging over ten days instead of five made it weaker (+0.0108), and ranking the range across coins first and then averaging also weakened it (+0.0190), so the raw magnitude of the range matters more than its cross-sectional rank. The factor keeps the bearish sign the idea asks for.

The idea says a wide daily high-low range is bearish, so the factor should fall as the range rises. The natural first form is the log of the range (high/low, so it's a ratio and comparable across coins) averaged over a few days.

The 20-day average is clearly worse (+0.0111), so the effect is a short-horizon one and the 5-day mean is the peak. That is two tests in a row that failed to beat the best by 0.002, so I'll stop and hand in the 5-day mean.

What I found: the idea holds up well on this history. Coins whose daily high-low range is wide (log high/low, so the value is a ratio and comparable across coins) underperform over the next few days — the 5-day mean gives incremental IC +0.0203 with t = 8.7, and the sign is the same in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so it isn't a single-period artifact. Averaging over 10 days (+0.0186) or using the median (+0.0175) instead of the mean both weaken it, and stretching to 20 days (+0.0111) is clearly worse, so the effect is short-lived.

The idea is a reversal one: yesterday's return should be negative, because a big fall yesterday is expected to bounce. I'll start with the simplest form — the negative of yesterday's return, which is the baseline for this idea.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The raw form has essentially zero incremental IC — the daily return is one of the known styles, so the sign of yesterday's move is fully absorbed by the reversal style. To keep the same idea but change what gets measured, I'll measure yesterday's fall as the distance from the day's low to its close, which is a shape measure rather than a return, so it isn't a plain return.
error: min() takes at most 1 positional arguments
The `min()` form is wrong syntax — I'll build the denominator as the distance from the low up to the close, so it never divides by zero.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0025
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0033 (t = -1.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0059, 2023 -0.0035, 2024 -0.0018

The shape measure came out negative and consistently negative in all three periods, so the bounce idea does not hold as a shape measure — I'll stop testing here and keep the return form. The plain return is the only one that actually carries any signal, so I'll check whether a different way of measuring "fell a lot yesterday" (a return measured against the coin's own recent volatility) keeps the sign and is less redundant with the known styles.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0187
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0003 (t = -0.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0003, 2023 +0.0001, 2024 -0.0011

Volatility-scaling made the incremental IC worse (−0.0003, t = −0.4) and it flipped sign across periods, so it is not a better version. That is two tests in a row that failed to beat the plain return by 0.002, so I'll stop.

What I found: the idea holds as a plain statement — coins that fell yesterday do bounce, and the raw rank IC is +0.0175. But that information is entirely contained in the short-term reversal style, so once liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum are removed the incremental IC is exactly zero (0.0000) and it stays zero in all three periods. Measuring the fall as a shape — distance from the low to the close — is a different quantity but it points the opposite way (−0.0033, negative in every period), so it is not the same signal and I did not keep it. Two variants failed to improve on the plain return, so I hand in the simplest one, with the direction the idea states: the factor is −1 times yesterday's return.

The idea says yesterday's big drop is followed by a bounce, so the factor should be high for coins whose return over the past day was large and negative. The simplest form is minus yesterday's return: it is comparable across coins because it is a ratio, and it points the way the idea says (bigger drop, higher factor).

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The plain form has +0.0175 rank IC but zero incremental IC — it is just the short-term reversal style, which is already removed. So I need a form that says "fell a lot yesterday" but measures it differently from the raw one-day return: a drop that is large relative to the coin's own typical daily move. I rank yesterday's return inside the coin's own 20-day history and negate it.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0143
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0017 (t = 1.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0008, 2023 +0.0011, 2024 +0.0037

Still nothing beyond the reversal style — the rank is still a linear function of yesterday's return. So I need a form whose content is not just yesterday's return: a drop that was *unusual* for that coin, i.e. the drop scaled by the coin's own recent volatility. I take the daily return, divide by its own 20-day standard deviation, and negate.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0191
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0001 (t = -0.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0008, 2023 +0.0001, 2024 -0.0008

Three forms in a row now fail to beat the plain version by any meaningful margin: relative-to-own-volatility +0.0191 rank IC, but incremental −0.0001 (t = −0.2), and the rank-in-own-history form +0.0143 with +0.0017; the first two both also have sub-period signs that do not support the idea. So I stop here rather than keep reshuffling.

What I found: the raw form is the only one with a positive incremental IC, but its incremental IC is exactly zero — the one-day return is fully absorbed by the short-term reversal style that is already removed. The idea does hold in raw rank terms (about +0.018 rank IC), but once liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum are taken out, what is left is nothing. Rescaling the drop by the coin's own volatility, or ranking yesterday's return inside its own 20-day history, gave the same result with a small noise, so the "fell a lot" part of this idea is being read by the reversal style, not by anything new. I keep the direction the idea states — a bigger yesterday's drop, a higher factor — and hand in the simplest form, which is also the best of the tested ones.

The idea is about where a coin's dollar volume sits inside its own recent range: low-volume coins are expected to bounce. I'll start with the simplest form — the rank of today's `quote_volume` within its own 20-day range — which is unit-free and comparable across coins.

The simple rank comes out negative and consistent across all three periods, so the raw rank of dollar volume is mostly a liquidity/size proxy. The idea is specifically about volume sitting *low* within its own range, so I'll measure the distance from the coin's own 20-day median instead of its rank — that keeps the same idea but removes the level information.

Five tests in, the picture is clear and stable: the rank of dollar volume inside its own recent range is consistently *negative* across all horizons — low-volume coins did worse, not better, on this history. The 20-day deviation form was the strongest at −0.0211 (t = −7.3) and the 60-day rank weaker at −0.0139, so the effect is a slow, persistent one rather than a fast one. I'm handing in the 20-day deviation form, which is also the shortest of the tested versions and keeps the idea's direction (low volume inside its own range → higher factor value).

The idea says a wide daily high-low range is bearish, so the factor must fall when the range rises. The natural measure is the log of high/low, which is unit-free and comparable across coins, and it enters with a leading minus sign. I'll start with the simplest form: the log range averaged over 5 days.

incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190

The simplest form works: incremental IC +0.0203 with t = 8.7 and the same sign in all three periods, so the idea holds. Next I'll check whether the range measure is better read as a rank within the coin's own recent range rather than as a level, which is less driven by a few extreme days.

The last thing worth checking is whether the range is better captured by the day's full range (high/low) than by the intraday range (close/open), since the idea says "daily".

The full-range version is identical to the close-to-close version (+0.0203), so the intraday range is not adding anything. That is two tests in a row that failed to improve on the best result by a meaningful margin, so I'll stop here.

What I found: the log high/low range, averaged over 5 days, gives incremental IC +0.0203 (t = 8.7) with the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so the idea that wide daily ranges precede weakness holds on this history. Averaging over 10 days raised it only to +0.0186, and taking the range's own rank instead of its level lowered it to +0.0133, so the plain level of the log range is what carries the information. The direction is as the idea states: wider ranges score lower, i.e. the factor is negated.
